extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, math educators, and researchers evaluating mathematical exposition and proof style
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate mathematical work (proofs, definitions, axiomatizations, and exposition) according to stylistic dimensions that affect understanding and future development: visualization, unification, axiom/definition choice, and the explicit acknowledgment of style. Used to judge explanatory/methodological quality beyond mere correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof's reliance (or non-reliance) on visualization: whether the proof is visualizable and supports geometric/intuitive understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualizable proofs support the reader's geometric intuition and tend to suggest extensions to similar geometric configurations; non-visualizable proofs are often more general but less supportive of pattern-based extension. The ideal (per Tappenden) is to offer the maximum visualization compatible with the result's generality. Choosing axioms that maximize visualizability is a legitimate research strategy. Score higher when visualization is exploited where compatible with generality; score lower when visualization is unnecessarily suppressed (e.g., for ideological reasons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the proof's framework groups the result with many other results (i.e., provides unification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs framed in unifying frameworks (e.g., category theory, gauge theory) place the result among many 'cousins' and reveal structural connections; proofs using highly specialized frameworks leave results isolated. Unification is a quality dimension distinct from beauty or formal rigor. Score higher when a proof meaningfully unifies results or when any isolation is acknowledged and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom Choice / Naturalness of Axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: How natural or artificial the chosen axioms/axiomatization appear, judged by how they support explanatory and efficient proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best axiom system is one that makes the deepest theorems quickest to prove; the best definitions support invariant structures across examples. A proof relying on artificial-looking axioms may indicate the framework is wrong even if the proof is formally correct. Prefer axiomatizations that yield short, explanatory proofs of deep results; penalize ones that require contortions to derive significant theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition Quality (right definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether definitions capture invariant structure across examples and serve explanatory and unifying roles rather than being ad hoc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good definitions: capture invariants across many examples; support short proofs of deep theorems; generalize naturally to higher dimensions or related contexts; make the right things equivalent and the right things distinct; survive independent rediscovery. Bad definitions: work only for the specific examples they were crafted for; require arbitrary choices; make deep results seem accidental; invite continual ad-hoc 'improvements.' Treat introducing a 'right' definition as a significant contribution in its own right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment of Stylistic Choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the author explicitly recognizes and discusses stylistic choices (presentation, axiomatization, visualization) and possible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work scores higher when stylistic choices are acknowledged and alternative styles or frameworks are noted. Work scores lower when stylistic choices are presented as inevitable or when alternative, possibly better, formulations are ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and Use of 'Good' Properties (Goodman-style criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work selects properties/classifications that are 'natural' (produce robust, fruitful classifications) rather than arbitrary ones that merely fit particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to Goodman's grue/green problem: many properties could organize an area, but only some yield natural classifications that support extensive theorem-proving. A proof or framework that identifies and employs such 'good' properties scores higher. The standard is objective but not derivable from logic alone; prefer properties that lead to productive mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing Definitions as Research Contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that finding the 'right'/'proper'/'natural' definition can itself be a primary research objective and a significant advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers that introduce a new, right definition may be more valuable than ones proving theorems using existing definitions. Evaluation should credit definition-making when it increases explanatory power, unification, or proof simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns / Lower-scoring Features
rubrics_metrics.description: Stylistic choices and features that indicate lower explanatory or methodological quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes suppression of visualization for irrelevant reasons; framework choices that unnecessarily isolate results; use of artificial axioms that require contortions; arbitrary definitions that fail to capture invariants; presenting style as inevitable rather than chosen; and definitions that work only for bespoke examples. Such features reduce a work's score even if proofs are correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to and Evaluation of AI-Generated Mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether automatically produced proofs and definitions satisfy the community standards for natural axioms and good definitions, not merely formal correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A machine may produce correct proofs that nonetheless use bad definitions or unnatural axioms; such output should be judged inferior. The rubric implies that assessment of AI-generated mathematics must include checks for definition quality, framework naturalness, visualization where appropriate, and unification — criteria that are currently difficult to automate.
